name: Chapter 13: Biodiversity and Conservation
description: Levels and numbers of biodiversity, latitudinal and species-area patterns, rivet popper, loss and evil quartet, in situ and ex situ conservation

Combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation, macromolecules to biomes

cards.text: Three important levels of biodiversity: {{c1::genetic}}, {{c2::species}} and {{c3::ecological}} diversity.

cards.term: Example of genetic diversity in a medicinal plant?
cards.definition: Rauwolfia vomitoria in different Himalayan ranges varies in potency and concentration of reserpine

cards.term: Genetic diversity in Indian rice and mango?
cards.definition: More than 50,000 rice strains and 1,000 mango varieties
Western Ghats have greater amphibian diversity than the Eastern Ghats
India (deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries, alpine meadows) > Norway

cards.term: How fast could we lose biodiversity?
cards.definition: In less than two centuries at present rates (it took millions of years to build)
Slightly more than 1.5 million

cards.term: How do ecologists estimate total species? (Exercise 2)
cards.definition: Compare temperate–tropical species richness of a well-studied insect group and extrapolate the ratio to other groups

cards.term: Robert May’s estimate of global species?
cards.definition: About 7 million (extreme estimates: 20–50 million)

cards.term: Share of animals and plants among recorded species?
cards.definition: Animals > 70%; plants (incl. algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms) ≤ 22%
Insects: > 70% of animals (7 of every 10 animals)

cards.term: Fungi vs vertebrates in species number?
cards.definition: Fungi species exceed the combined total of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals
Conventional taxonomy unsuitable; many are not culturable; by molecular criteria they may run into millions

cards.term: Largest slice in the vertebrate pie?
cards.definition: Fishes

cards.term: Largest slices in the plant pie?
cards.definition: Angiosperms and fungi

cards.term: India’s share of land vs species?
cards.definition: 2.4% of land area but 8.1% of global species diversity
One of the 12 mega diversity countries
Nearly 45,000 plants and twice as many animals
More than 1,00,000 plants and 3,00,000 animals (only 22% recorded, by May’s estimate)
Species are going extinct before we even discover and catalogue them

cards.term: Why do animals outnumber plants in species? (Exercise 9)
cards.definition: Mobility, varied niches and body plans, rapid breeding and huge insect radiation (flight, small size, metamorphosis)
Species diversity decreases from the equator towards the poles
23.5° N to 23.5° S
Colombia (near equator): nearly 1,400; New York (41° N): 105; Greenland (71° N): 56; India: more than 1,200

cards.term: Tropical vs temperate forest plant diversity?
cards.definition: Ecuador forest has up to 10 times vascular plant species of a same-size Midwest USA forest

cards.term: Place with the greatest biodiversity on earth?
cards.definition: The Amazonian rain forest
Plants: > 40,000; Fishes: 3,000; Birds: 1,300; Mammals: 427; Amphibians: 427; Reptiles: 378; Invertebrates: > 1,25,000
(a) More evolutionary time (no glaciations) (b) less seasonal, constant environment → niche specialisation (c) more solar energy → higher productivity
"Time, Tranquillity, Tan": more time, stable climate, more sunshine
Alexander von Humboldt in South American jungles
Rectangular hyperbola; a straight line on a log–log scale
\( \log S = \log C + Z \log A \) (i.e. \( S = CA^Z \))
S: Species richness; A: Area; Z: Slope (regression coefficient); C: Y-intercept

cards.definition: 0.1 to 0.2, regardless of taxon or region

cards.term: Z for very large areas like continents?
cards.definition: Much steeper: 0.6 to 1.2; frugivorous birds and mammals of tropical forests 1.15
Species richness rises faster with area; losing area loses species much faster
Little year-to-year variation in productivity; resistant or resilient to disturbance; resistant to alien invasions
Plots with more species had less year-to-year biomass variation and higher productivity

cards.term: Rivet popper hypothesis: who and analogy?
cards.definition: Paul Ehrlich: airplane = ecosystem; rivets = species

cards.term: Lessons of the rivet popper hypothesis?
cards.definition: Losing a few rivets may not matter at first, but many weakens the plane; losing key rivets on wings (key species) is most dangerous

cards.term: How is biodiversity important for ecosystems (Exercise 6)?
cards.definition: More species → stability, productivity, resistance to invasion and disturbance, ecosystem services

cards.term: Birds lost by human colonisation of Pacific islands?
cards.definition: More than 2,000 native bird species

cards.term: IUCN Red List 2004 extinctions in last 500 years?
cards.definition: 784 species: 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates, 87 plants
Dodo: Mauritius; Quagga: Africa; Thylacine: Australia; Steller’s sea cow: Russia; Tiger subspecies (Bali, Javan, Caspian): Asia

cards.term: Extinctions in the last twenty years (NCERT)?
cards.definition: 27 species
Amphibians
More than 15,500
Birds: 12%; Mammals: 23%; Amphibians: 32%; Gymnosperms: 31%

cards.term: Update: how many species are threatened today?
cards.definition: IUCN Red List now lists over 44,000 threatened species (2024); NCERT’s 15,500 is from 2004

cards.term: How many mass extinctions in earth’s history?
cards.definition: Five (over > 3 billion years)
Rates are 100–1,000 times faster than pre-human times, due to human activities
Nearly half of all species within 100 years

cards.term: Effects of biodiversity loss in a region?
cards.definition: Decline in plant production; lower resistance to perturbations (drought); more variable productivity, water use, pest and disease cycles

cards.text: The "Evil Quartet" of biodiversity loss: {{c1::habitat loss and fragmentation}}, {{c2::over-exploitation}}, {{c3::alien species invasions}}, {{c4::co-extinctions}}.

cards.definition: "HOPE" lost: Habitat loss, Over-exploitation, Pests/alien invaders, Extinction partners (co-extinction)
Habitat loss and fragmentation

cards.term: Tropical rain forest cover then and now?
cards.definition: Once > 14% of land; now ≤ 6%

cards.term: Why is Amazon called the "lungs of the planet"?
cards.definition: Huge rain forest estimated to produce 20% of atmospheric oxygen

cards.term: Why is the Amazon being cleared?
cards.definition: For soya beans and grassland for beef cattle
Mammals and birds needing large territories, and migratory animals
Steller’s sea cow, passenger pigeon; over-harvested marine fish
Over-exploitation
Introduced into Lake Victoria → extinction of > 200 species of cichlid fish
Parthenium (carrot grass), Lantana, water hyacinth (Eichhornia)
Eichhornia
African catfish Clarias gariepinus (illegal introduction for aquaculture)
Obligately associated species die with the host: a fish’s unique parasites; a coevolved plant–pollinator pair

cards.term: Major causes of species loss in a region (Exercise 5)?
cards.definition: The Evil Quartet: habitat loss/fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien invasions, co-extinctions

cards.text: Reasons to conserve biodiversity: {{c1::narrowly utilitarian}}, {{c2::broadly utilitarian}}, and {{c3::ethical}}.

cards.definition: Direct economic benefits: food, firewood, fibre, construction, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes), medicines
More than 25% of drugs sold worldwide; 25,000 plant species in traditional medicine
Exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance
Ecosystem services: oxygen (Amazon ~20%), pollination, aesthetic pleasures
Every species has intrinsic value; moral duty to pass on our biological legacy

cards.term: How do biotic components control floods and erosion? (Exercise 8)
cards.definition: Plant roots bind soil, vegetation and litter slow runoff and increase water infiltration
On-site: protecting the whole ecosystem; "save the entire forest to save the tiger"

cards.term: What is ex situ conservation, and when used?
cards.definition: Off-site: threatened species taken out for special care; when species are endangered and need urgent measures
Regions with very high species richness and high endemism; also regions of accelerated habitat loss
Species confined to a region and found nowhere else
Initially 25, then 9 added → 34
36 (two more added after NCERT’s count)
Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya

cards.term: Land area and impact of hotspots?
cards.definition: Less than 2% of land; strict protection could reduce mass extinctions by ~30%
14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks, 448 wildlife sanctuaries
About 18 biosphere reserves, 106 national parks and over 570 sanctuaries (numbers keep growing)
Forest tracts set aside by religious/cultural tradition where all trees and wildlife are venerated and protected; refuges for rare species
Meghalaya: Khasi and Jaintia Hills; Rajasthan: Aravalli Hills; Karnataka, Maharashtra: Western Ghats; Madhya Pradesh: Sarguja, Chanda, Bastar

Zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks

In situ = "in its site" (parks, reserves, sacred groves). Ex situ = "exit the site" (zoos, gardens, seed banks).
Convention on Biological Diversity, Rio de Janeiro, 1992
2002, Johannesburg: 190 countries pledged significant reduction of biodiversity loss by 2010

cards.term: Update: were the 2010 targets met, and what now?
cards.definition: No; the 2022 Kunming–Montreal framework aims to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030 ("30×30")

cards.term: When might we want a species extinct? (Exercise 10)
cards.definition: Disease-causing organisms, e.g. the smallpox virus or polio virus, to protect human health

cards.definition: National park: In situ; Sacred grove: In situ; Biosphere reserve: In situ; Zoo: Ex situ; Seed bank: Ex situ; Cryopreserved gametes: Ex situ
